content.title: About
content.content: Paratha is an Indian flatbread made from whole‑wheat or white flour, water, salt and sometimes clarified butter (ghee) or oil. The dough is rolled into thin circles and cooked on a hot skillet until golden brown. Paratha can be plain or stuffed with vegetables, potatoes, cheese, and other fillings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Paratha is commonly served with curry, dal or chutney in Indian cuisine.
There are over 100 varieties of paratha, including layered and flaky versions.
Traditionally the dough is rested to relax gluten, resulting in a softer bread.
In some regions yogurt is added to the dough, making it puffier.
Paratha is a popular street‑food item because it cooks quickly and is served hot.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Paratha provides steady energy through slowly digestible carbs, helping maintain blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Contains plant protein
items.content: The flour used supplies protein important for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B3 and B6 support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Beneficial fats when cooked with ghee
items.content: Ghee adds short‑chain fatty acids that are easily absorbed.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: A rested dough develops mild probiotic qualities that aid gut health.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Paratha, especially when cooked with oil, is calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should avoid traditional paratha.

items.title: Salt level
items.content: Excessive salt in the dough can contribute to high blood pressure.

items.title: Frying adds fat
items.content: Cooking on a skillet with oil increases fat intake, which may be undesirable on low‑fat diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Paratha is eaten hot, either rolled up, folded, or cut into pieces. It is served with curry, chutney, yogurt, and can be used as a sandwich base. Fillings such as vegetables, potatoes or cheese can be added before folding.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked paratha in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage keep it in the refrigerator (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Reheat on a dry skillet to restore crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Cocktail sauce is a thick, flavorful condiment typically made from tomato ketchup, horseradish, lemon juice, Worcestershire sauce, and spices. It is traditionally served with seafood, especially shrimp cocktail, but also works as a dip for fish, chicken, and vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first cocktail sauce recipes appeared in the United States in the early 20th century.
The classic American version contains horseradish, while European variants often replace it with Worcestershire or soy sauce.
Cocktail sauce is commonly served in small glasses alongside shrimp cocktail in seafood restaurants.
Many variations exist: spicier versions add Tabasco, sweeter ones incorporate honey or brown sugar.
In Japan a popular version mixes soy sauce, rice vinegar, and wasabi.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Lemon juice provides vitamin C, which supports the immune system.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Tomato ketchup and horseradish supply lycopene and glucosinolates with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Horseradish can stimulate bile production, potentially improving digestion.

items.title: High sugar and salt content
items.content: Ketchup and ready-made sauces often contain significant amounts of sugar and sodium, which may be problematic for hypertension or diabetes.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: While the sauce itself does not contain shellfish, it is usually served with them, posing a risk for allergic individuals.

items.title: Spicy horseradish
items.content: Horseradish can irritate the stomach lining in people with sensitivity.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Serve the sauce with cold seafood (shrimp cocktail, crab sticks), use as a dip for fried fish, chicken nuggets, or vegetable sticks. It can also be added to marinades, salad dressings, or used as a base for more complex sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep opened cocktail sauce refrigerated in a sealed container. It stays fresh for 1–2 weeks. Discard if you notice off‑smell, color changes, or mold.

fruit-salad-excluding-citrus-fruits-with.title: Fruit Salad without Citrus with Pudding

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit salad without citrus with pudding is a mix of fresh berries, apples, pears, bananas and other non‑citrus fruits, tossed with a smooth vanilla pudding (item 4061). The salad is served chilled and works as a light dessert or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The salad contains no citrus, making it safe for people allergic to lemon, orange or grapefruit.
The pudding base is made from milk, starch and vanilla extract, giving the dish a creamy texture.
Apples and pears stay crisp thanks to a short chill time in the refrigerator.
Bananas add natural sweetness, allowing the recipe to use less added sugar.
The dish can be prepared in 15‑20 minutes, which is why it’s popular in cafés and cafeterias.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Apples, pears and bananas provide vitamins B1, B2 and B6, supporting metabolic processes.

items.title: Good source of dietary fiber
items.content: The fruit mix supplies soluble and insoluble fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The salad contains almost no fat, and the pudding is made with skim milk, keeping it light.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Berries such as blueberries and strawberries are high in anthocyanins, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C from the berries (non‑citrus) helps boost the immune system.

items.title: Allergy to specific fruits
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to apples, pears or certain berries; a test portion is advisable.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Bananas and berries are naturally sweet, so people monitoring blood glucose should consider the total carbohydrate load.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Certain fruits can increase stomach acidity; those with gastritis should choose milder options.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled in individual cups or bowls. Before serving, garnish with fresh mint leaves or a sprinkle of chopped nuts for extra crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. The pudding may separate, so give it a gentle stir before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Grapes are small, juicy, sweet berries that grow in clusters on the vines of Vitis vinifera and related species, cultivated for thousands of years. They come in green, red, purple, and black varieties, seeded and seedless. Grapes are eaten fresh, dried as raisins, and made into juice, wine, and vinegar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Grapes are among the oldest cultivated fruits, with a history of at least several thousand years.
Raisins are dried grapes, and currants and sultanas are types of dried grapes.
Grapes are used to make wine, juice, jams, and vinegar.
Red and purple grapes contain resveratrol and other polyphenols, mostly in the skin.
Grapes do not ripen after being picked, so they are harvested when ripe.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: Grapes, especially red and purple ones, contain resveratrol and anthocyanins with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Provides vitamin K and vitamin C
items.content: These vitamins support blood clotting and the immune system.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Hydrating
items.content: Grapes are high in water and a refreshing snack.

items.title: Convenient
items.content: Grapes are portable and need no preparation.

items.title: Natural sugar content
items.content: Grapes contain natural sugars, so portions matter for people monitoring blood sugar.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole grapes are a choking hazard for young children and should be cut lengthwise.

items.title: Toxic to dogs
items.content: Grapes and raisins are toxic to dogs and can cause kidney damage, so keep them away from pets.

items.title: Pesticide residues and allergies
items.content: Wash grapes before eating. Allergy to grapes is uncommon but can occur.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Grapes can be eaten fresh as a snack, added to fruit and chicken salads, frozen as a cool treat, or roasted. They can be pressed into juice or dried into raisins. Choose whole grapes over juice for more fiber.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unwashed grapes in the refrigerator in a breathable bag or container, where they usually keep for one to two weeks. Wash them just before eating. Remove any soft or moldy grapes. Grapes can also be frozen.

green-beans-canned-cooked-with-butter-or.title: Green beans canned, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Canned green beans cooked in butter or margarine are selected bean pods that are blanched, sterilized and sealed in a jar with butter. The product is ready to eat, has a mild buttery flavor and retains most of its nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green beans are one of the most popular vegetables for canning because of their texture and taste.
In the United States the beans are traditionally cooked in butter, while some countries use margarine to reduce cost.
Canning allows storage for 2–3 years without loss of flavor.
Vitamin K levels in canned beans can be higher than in fresh beans due to the heat process.
Canned green beans are a common staple for camping and long trips as a vegetable source.

items.title: Good source of plant protein
items.content: Green beans provide about 2–3 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps you feel full.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Canned beans retain thiamine (B1), pyridoxine (B6) and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: They contain iron, magnesium and potassium, which support heart and nerve function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Polysaccharides and flavonoids in beans help combat free radicals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned foods often contain added salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Cooking in butter raises the calorie count; those monitoring weight should consider this.

items.title: Bisphenol A
items.content: Some cans may be lined with epoxy resins; choose products from reputable manufacturers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The beans are ready straight from the jar: add them to salads, soups, stews, or serve as a side dish. They can also be quickly warmed in a pan with extra herbs or spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the beans in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 3–4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Pea salad is a dish made from boiled or canned green peas, often combined with vegetables, herbs, mayonnaise or a light yogurt‑based dressing. It has a mildly sweet flavor and a crunchy texture, suitable as a side dish or a light main course.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peas are one of the oldest legume crops, cultivated for over 7,000 years.
There are more than 30 varieties of peas, including sweet, garden, and snap peas.
Peas are a good source of plant protein and are widely used in vegetarian diets.
In many traditional cuisines (e.g., Russian, Polish, Indian) pea salad is a classic comfort food.
Dried peas can be stored for several years when kept in a cool, dry place.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Peas provide about 5 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion and helps maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Peas contain vitamin B6, folate, and thiamine, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: They supply iron, magnesium, phosphorus and zinc, supporting blood and bone health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Peas raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for weight control and diabetes management.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Legumes can cause increased gas in sensitive people.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid may reduce mineral absorption; soaking or sprouting can mitigate this.

items.title: Sodium in prepared salad
items.content: If the salad is dressed with mayonnaise or soy sauce, sodium levels can be high.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve pea salad chilled as an appetizer, a side to meat or fish, or as a light meal. Enhance it with boiled eggs, ham, fresh vegetables, herbs, and a simple dressing of yogurt, lemon juice and olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. If storing without dressing, keep the peas and vegetables separate to preserve freshness.

content.title: About
content.content: Mashed potato NFS is a ready‑to‑eat product made from selected potatoes processed with the “Non‑Fried Spray” (NFS) technology. The mash has a smooth, creamy texture, a mild buttery flavor, and retains most of the nutrients of the original potato.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The NFS process preserves up to 90 % of vitamin C, which is often lost in conventional cooking.
The mash is produced without artificial preservatives or colorants.
One serving (100 g) provides about 80 kcal, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.
Potatoes used for NFS are grown in environmentally controlled regions without genetically modified seeds.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain normal fluid balance and supports healthy heart function.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that supports immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The mash contains less than 0.2 g of fat per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Provides vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience an allergic reaction to potatoes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some variants may contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes have a high glycemic index, so those with diabetes should consider portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the mash in a microwave or on the stovetop, then stir in butter, milk, cheese, or herbs to taste. It works well as a side dish for meat, fish, or vegetable plates.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the mash refrigerated at 0 °C – 4 °C in its original packaging. Once opened, consume within 3 days. Discard if any off‑odor or discoloration appears.
